Dear Eric
After spending some time lookin at the reorg listener interface in full_node*,  I realize that the distinction of the process of the header sync (which is happening conceptually first: header-first sync, right) versus block sync, is not clear to me.

Is LibBitcoin somehow integrating these two into one, so that there is only one reorg listener and event stream, and not two?

How does that work out in practice.

Is it that the reorg logics in LibBitcoin are trigged based on the headers only - and the reorg listener is trigged accordingly - and these logics *presume* that there will be data availability of the blocks in this chain,  such that get/fetch/downloaded block listener events are presumed to follow for each block?

Please explain

elements.text:
Hi Phil,

If you are looking at header sync, you are in v4.

In v4 the process is as follows. First, the structure:

The block table retains headers (a bit of a misnomer), the tx table retains txs. There is an association table that retains the associations between headers and their downloaded transactions. The purpose of the association is to allow headers (before obtaining txs) to be stored in an array-table, as the association to txs is fixed-width. There are two height indexes, one for the confirmed chain and one for a candidate chain. The confirmed index is authoritative for the strong branch. The candidate index is the next-strongest visible branch. There are arrays of pointers to block headers, allowing blocks to be queried by height in constant time. There is also a payments index. This provides constant time query from any output script to the transactions that contains it (outputs) and any that reference it (inputs). The indexes are redundant information. The entire chain is retained by the three headers->transactions tables. Headers can exist without associated transactions, and transactions can exist without associating headers. Transactions can be associated by any number of headers. All associations are complete (full block or none)...

elements.text: Data is stored as soon as the cost of producing invalid data reaches an arbitrary threshold. This is a denial-of-service feature. For headers this is specified in config as an amount of time from the present clock. The header chain must reach this relative height before block downloading begins. This is referred to as being "current". If the header chain is not current, no blocks are downloaded. If there is a current header, all headers preceding it are downloaded in parallel. They are stored as txs and associations as that happens. This is performed entirely independent of order. Standard deviation is used to detect slower peers in the block downloading, which are disconnected if they fall below a configurable threshold. This results in an acceleration of downloading, and unloads peers that appear to be overloaded. This is not done by header downloading, as we want all peers to have an opportunity to define the strong chain, so header download tends to be slow relative to the amount of data processed.

elements.text: This process is not independent. Header download proceeds alongside block download. But block download only occurs when there are "current" headers that have not been populated by block download. I refer to this as continuous parallel block download.

elements.text:
Specifically, I though, what if a malicious miner would produce many block headers but for blocks that don’t exist.

If LibBitcoin’s header and block sync process are one, where the header sync part decides which is the longest chain and block download is then applied on those blocks, if this is how the block sync works then essentially LibBitcoin block sync is stalled during any such >50% malicious miners attack which does an unavailable blocks attack.

For this reason I originally assumed that LibBitcoin would have two separate sync processes internally: one separate header sync process, which is about finding the longest header chain. But then a separate block sync process which will cause LibBitcoin to use as actually longest chain, the longest chain for which it has blocks, too. This approach would render LibBitcoin resistant to the attack I described.

However, I do see the argument that “header only & block unavailable attack” is unreasonable.
